rationale: A wins because it keeps three real stories separate and refuses to decorate holes with borrowed trend furniture. "The AI travel planner that books nothing" is sharp, defensible, and immediately tells a reporter what to test. B has one strong idea in "fare alert, not a chat prompt," but then it drifts into unsupported scenery like "Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper" and pads with "The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app," which is a profile wish wearing a news hat.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief, loudly marketed across the industry" needs outside proof; A flags that partly, but the line still leans on an unsourced market narrative.
"alert-to-itinerary" as a possible product category is useful, but it needs competitor context before anyone should pitch it as category creation.
The set misses B's strongest product-design contrast: fare-alert-triggered planning versus chat-prompt planning.
gaps_in_B: "Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products" is not in the update. It may be true, but in this exercise it is imported scaffolding.
"most AI trip planners start from a user's query" is the best angle in B, but it is also an unverified comparison claim and needs proof before it becomes the spine of a pitch.
"The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app" is padded biography. The update only gives the former name, not a supported identity-arc story.
"travel-tech product reporter at a trade outlet" and "tech reporter or columnist" are weaker journalist shapes than A's tighter consumer-travel-tech, subscription-value, and travel-tech lanes.
